summary: Fraction notation a/b is a compact language naming a SINGLE number: the denominator says how many equal parts one whole is split into, and the numerator counts how many of those parts we have. Teach the vocabulary in use, always anchored to a model (bar, circle, number line), and deliberately stretch the language to name unit (1/b), proper (a<b), improper (a>=b) and mixed numbers so children meet the full grammar early rather than believing 'you can't have 5/4'. A proposed emphasis is on GENERATING notation (shade N of M equal parts and watch the symbol form) so the symbol is tied to an amount, rather than only memorising top/bottom labels.
misconceptions: Reads 3/4 as two separate whole numbers ('three, four') rather than one quantity
Writes the fraction upside down — swaps numerator and denominator
Believes an improper fraction like 5/4 or 4/3 'isn't a real number / can't exist'
Mixes the vocabulary — calls the bottom number the numerator
Thinks 2/4 and 1/2 must be different amounts because the numbers differ

activities.title: Build the fraction, build the name
steps: Cut a bar into M equal parts (for example set it to 4) and shade N of them (for example 3), then write the symbol that matches: the parts taken on top, the equal parts in one whole on the bottom.
As you shade, say the fraction as one spoken quantity ('three-quarters'), not 'three, four'.
Label each number to its job: the numerator is 'the 3 parts we took' and the denominator is 'the 4 equal parts in one whole'.

Now push the numerator past the denominator (shade 5 parts when the whole holds 4): the shading overflows into a second whole. Record that this is called an improper fraction (5/4) and write its mixed twin beside it (1 1/4).

Sort every fraction you build into four trays: unit (numerator 1 and denominator more than 1, like 1/4), proper-but-not-unit (numerator more than 1 but less than the denominator, like 3/4), improper (numerator as big as or bigger than the denominator, like 5/4 or 4/4; 1/1 also goes here because it equals one whole), and mixed (like 1 1/4). A unit fraction like 1/4 is a special kind of proper fraction, so sort each card into its most specific tray.

Shade 2/4 of a bar, then slide that shaded length to overlay 1/2 of a bar of the same length (the same whole): notice the symbols differ but the shaded length is identical, so they name the same amount.
activities.insight: Fraction notation names one number. The bottom number tells how many equal parts one whole is cut into; the top counts how many we have. Pushing the numerator past the denominator shows 5/4 is a real number greater than one (equal to 1 1/4), and overlaying 2/4 on 1/2 shows different symbols can name the same quantity.

activities.title: Label the fraction's jobs
steps: Look at 3/4 beside its shaded bar. Point to the numerator and say what it does ('the parts we took'); point to the denominator and say what it does ('the equal parts in one whole').
Point to the whole bar and explain it is the one whole that was cut up.
Answer the prompt 'What if the top number were bigger than the bottom?' and predict what the picture and the name would become.
Link the three forms both directions: write the symbol, say the words, shade the picture, and go back again.
activities.insight: Each part of the written symbol has a fixed job tied to the model, and the symbol, spoken words and diagram are three views of the same single quantity.

activities.title: Classify and match for fluency
steps: Sort a set of fraction cards into unit, proper, improper and mixed, giving one example of each; remember a unit fraction (numerator 1, denominator more than 1, like 1/4) is a special kind of proper fraction, so place it in the unit tray and keep the proper tray for proper fractions whose numerator is greater than 1 (a card such as 1/1 equals one whole and goes in the improper tray).
Match spoken words to written symbols (for example 'three-quarters' to 3/4).
Fill in the missing number: a shaded picture shows ?/? parts; write both the numerator and the denominator.
Explain in your own words why 2/4 and 1/2 are equivalent.
activities.insight: Secure classification and word-symbol matching show the vocabulary has attached to structure, not just to top/bottom positions.

checkQuestion: Here is a pizza cut into 8 equal slices, and you eat 3 of them. Write that as a fraction, and as you write it tell me what each number in it stands for. Then I have written 5/4 on the board for a recipe — read it aloud for me and tell me what it means, and whether writing a fraction like that is allowed.
checkAnswer: Writes 3/8; says the bottom number 8 (denominator) is the number of equal slices the whole pizza was cut into and the top number 3 (numerator) is how many of those slices were eaten. Reads 5/4 as 'five-quarters' (five-fourths), explains it means five parts each a quarter, which is more than one whole (one whole and one more quarter, 1 1/4), and yes it is allowed — an improper fraction is still a single number.
